summary: This informational memo covers what application developers should consider when moving to IPv6. It describes scenarios and aspects of application transition and gives guidelines for writing programs that work with IPv6, IPv4, or both.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving to IPv6 is not only a job for routers and network engineers. The programs people run also have to be able to talk over IPv6, and they have to keep working when only one of the two protocols is available. RFC 4038 sorts out the cases, lists what usually goes wrong, and gives concrete advice on writing code that does not care which version of IP it is running over.

questions: how to make applications support ipv6
what is a dual stack application
how do i port an application to ipv6
what is ipv4 mapped ipv6 address
subtitle: What a program has to change so that it works over IPv4, over IPv6, and over both.

tldr.problem: The mechanisms that let IPv4 and IPv6 networks coexist say nothing about whether the programs running on those machines can speak IPv6, and a program that only knows about IPv4 will simply fail to reach some hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The memo classifies application transition into four cases, names the three problems that make it awkward, and then gives porting guidelines: use the address-independent socket calls, ask the resolver for every address, and try each returned address until one works.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo. Its advice is to write one program that works with both protocols rather than two programs that work with one each, and to try every address the resolver returns rather than only the first.

today: RFC 4038 is an Informational memo published in March 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives porting guidance for applications during the IPv6 transition, using the socket interface extensions of RFC 3493 and RFC 3542.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
As IPv6 is introduced into the IPv4-based Internet, several general issues arise, such as routing, addressing, DNS, and scenarios. An important key to a successful IPv6 transition is compatibility with the large installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers. That issue has been studied extensively and work is still in progress. The basic transition mechanisms, dual-stack deployment and tunneling, are described in the IPv6 host and router transition work, and various other kinds of mechanism have been developed since. Those mechanisms, however, take no stance on whether applications support IPv6.

RFC 4038 covers the application side of the transition, in two inter-related parts. The first is how the different network transition techniques affect applications, and what strategies an application can use to support IPv6 and IPv4. The second is how to develop IPv6-capable, or protocol-independent, applications, which it calls application porting guidelines, using the standard socket interface extensions in RFC 3493 and RFC 3542.

The term application covers all kinds of applications, but the focus is on network applications developed with relatively low-level APIs, such as the C language with standard libraries. Many of them could be command-line driven, but that is not a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers and the network can be ready for IPv6 while the programs are not, and that mismatch is what breaks things. This memo is about the programs: how to write one that works whichever version of IP it ends up using.

sections.title: The Four Cases of Application Transition
sections.content:
The transition of an application is classified by four cases, excluding the case where there is no IPv6 support at all in either the application or the operating system.

Case 1 is IPv4-only applications in a dual-stack node. The IPv6 protocol is introduced in a node, but the applications are not yet ported to support IPv6, so the node has both protocol stacks and one kind of application.

Case 2 is IPv4-only applications and IPv6-only applications in a dual-stack node. The applications are ported for IPv6 only, so there are two similar applications, one for each protocol version, for example ping and ping6.

Case 3 is applications supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 in a dual-stack node. The applications are ported for both, so the existing IPv4 applications can be removed and there is one version of each.

Case 4 is applications supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 in an IPv4-only node. The applications are ported for both, but the same applications also have to work when IPv6 is not being used, for example because it has been disabled in the operating system.

The memo says the first two cases are not interesting in the longer term. Only a few applications are inherently IPv4-specific or IPv6-specific, and those should work with both protocols without having to care about which one is being used.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four situations: an old program on a new machine, two programs on a new machine, one program that does both on a new machine, and one program that does both on an old machine. The memo is mainly interested in the last two.

sections.title: Why the Transition Is Hard
sections.content:
The memo names three problems that make the transition period between IPv4 and IPv6 applications less than straightforward.

The first is that IPv6 support in the operating system and in applications are unrelated. IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks are likely to co-exist in a node for a long time, and most applications are expected to be able to handle both for another long period. A dual-stack operating system is not intended to have both IPv4 and IPv6 applications, so the transition of an application to be IPv6-capable may be independent of the protocol stacks in the node. Applications capable of both IPv4 and IPv6 will probably have to work properly in IPv4-only nodes, whether the IPv6 protocol is completely disabled or there is no IPv6 connectivity at all.

The second is that DNS does not indicate which IP version will be used. In a node the DNS name resolver gathers the list of destination addresses, and the queries and responses travel over either IPv4 or IPv6 regardless of the protocol version of the data records. By only doing a DNS name lookup, a client application cannot be certain of the version of the peer application. The example given is a server application that does not support IPv6 yet but runs on a dual-stack machine for other IPv6 services: if that host is listed with an AAAA record, the client application will fail to connect, because the DNS query result and the server application's version do not match. SRV records would avoid these problems, but they are not used widely enough to be applicable in most cases, so the operational answer is to use service names in the DNS, adding a name for each service or group of services that is offered over IPv6, with the associated A and AAAA records, rather than a single name for the physical machine. Applications cannot depend on that operational practice. The application should request all IP addresses without address family constraints and try all the records returned from the DNS, in some order, until a working address is found, and it has to be able to handle all IP versions returned.

The third is that supporting many versions of an application is difficult. System administrators may have various versions of the same application available, and typically one cannot know which IP versions must be supported before doing a DNS lookup and trying the addresses returned. If multiple versions are available, local users have difficulty selecting the right one. To avoid a program not supporting the specified protocol version, it is desirable to have hybrid applications supporting both. The alternative is a wrapper application that works out which protocol version will be used, makes the connection, and passes the opened socket to another application. The memo rejects that idea: such applications become complex, likely much more so than a hybrid application, and writing wrappers that perform complex operations with IP addresses, such as FTP clients, might be even more challenging or impossible. Wrapper applications do not look like a robust approach for application transition.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things get in the way. A machine can run IPv6 while the program on it does not know about IPv6. The name in DNS does not say which version will be used, so a lookup can hand back an address the other end cannot accept. And having two versions of the same program to choose from is a mess for the people who have to pick one.

sections.title: How Each Case Behaves
sections.content:
Once the IPv6 network is deployed, applications supporting IPv6 can use IPv6 network services to establish IPv6 connections. Upgrading every node to IPv6 at the same time is not feasible, and the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 will be gradual, so dual-stack nodes provide one way of keeping IPv4 compatibility for unicast communications.

In Case 1, the IPv6 protocol has been added to a node but IPv6-capable applications are not yet available or installed. The node implements the dual stack, but IPv4 applications can only manage IPv4 communications. The first priority is to port applications to IPv6. In some cases, for example when no source code is available, existing IPv4 applications can work if the Bump-in-the-Stack or Bump-in-the-API mechanism is installed in the node, but the memo strongly recommends that developers not use these mechanisms when source code is available, and that they not be used as an excuse not to port software or to delay porting. When they are used, the DNS problem described in section 3 arises, but one can rely on the mechanism cycling through all the addresses instead of the applications. These mechanisms do not work with all kinds of applications, in particular with applications that exchange IP addresses as application data, such as FTP: they give the applications IPv4 temporary addresses and make the translation between IPv4 and IPv6 locally, so those addresses are only valid inside the node.

In Case 2, the easiest way to port an IPv4 application is to substitute the old IPv4 API references with the new IPv6 APIs one for one, which makes the application IPv6-only. Such code cannot work in IPv4-only nodes, so the old IPv4 application has to be kept there too, which means two similar applications depending on the node they run on, for example telnet and telnet6. The memo calls this case undesirable. Most implementations of dual stack let IPv6-only applications interoperate with both IPv4 and IPv6 nodes, because IPv4 packets going to IPv6 applications on a dual-stack node reach their destination through IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses: the IPv6 address ::FFFF:x.y.z.w represents the IPv4 address x.y.z.w. For an IPv6-only server, an IPv4 client sending to the wildcard address has its address read as the IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, so the IPv6 application manages the communication as a usual IPv6 connection, although IPv4 packets are exchanged between the nodes. For an IPv6-only client, IPv4-mapped addresses are not returned by the hostname resolution functions unless the special hint AI_V4MAPPED is given. With IPV6_V6ONLY set, an IPv6-only server will talk only to IPv6 nodes and an IPv6-only client only to IPv6 servers, because the mapped addresses are disabled; the option is useful when an application uses new IPv6 features such as the Flow Label. Some implementations of dual stack do not allow IPv4-mapped addresses to be used for interoperability at all, and the two ways of handling that are to deploy two different versions of the application, possibly with a 6 in the name, or to deploy one application supporting both protocol versions. The first is not recommended because of the problems of selecting the right application.

In Case 3, applications are ported to support both IPv4 and IPv6, and over time the existing IPv4-only applications can be removed. Because there is only one version of each application, the source code is typically easy to maintain and modify, and there is no problem of managing which application to select. The memo calls this the most advisable transition case. Applications supporting both should be able to communicate with other applications irrespective of the version of the protocol stack or the application in the node. If the source code is written in a protocol-independent way, without dependencies on either IPv4 or IPv6, applications will be able to communicate with any combination of applications and node types. Implementations typically prefer IPv6 by default if the remote node and application support it, and if IPv6 connections fail, version-independent applications will automatically try IPv4 ones: the resolver returns a list of valid addresses, and the application iterates through all of them until the connection succeeds. Application writers should be aware of this protocol ordering, which is typically the default, though the applications usually need not be. If the source code is written in a protocol-dependent way, the application supports IPv4 and IPv6 explicitly by using two separate sockets, and there are differences in the bind() implementation, in whether one can first bind to IPv6 wildcard addresses and then to those for IPv4. Writing applications that cope with this can be a pain, and implementing IPV6_V6ONLY simplifies it. The IPv4 wildcard bind fails on some systems because the IPv4 address space is embedded into the IPv6 address space when IPv4-mapped addresses are used.

In Case 4, the transition is likely to take place over a longer time frame, so applications already ported to support both may be run on IPv4-only nodes, typically to avoid supporting two application versions for older and newer operating systems, or to support a case where the user wants to disable IPv6. The most important case is where IPv6 support can be dynamically enabled or disabled by the user, and the application has to handle the situation where IPv6 would not be enabled. Another scenario is deployment on older systems that do not support IPv6 at all, even the basic APIs such as getaddrinfo(), where the designer has to make a case-by-case judgment call about whether to have a compile-time toggle between an older and a newer API, or to provide getaddrinfo() support on older platforms as part of the application libraries. The example given is an application that issues a socket() call, trying AF_INET6 and then AF_INET. If the kernel has no IPv6 support, the call results in an EPROTONOSUPPORT or EAFNOSUPPORT error, and such errors typically lead to exiting the socket loop, so AF_INET is not even tried. The application has to handle that case, or build the loop so that errors are ignored until the last address family.

The memo closes the transition discussion with a note on mechanism. The NAT-PT mechanism introduces a special set of addresses, formed of a NAT-PT prefix and an IPv4 address, that refer to IPv4 addresses translated by the NAT-PT DNS-ALG. IPv6 applications must not be required to distinguish normal addresses from NAT-PT translated ones, or from any other kind of special address, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. That would be completely impractical, and if the distinction must be made, it must be done elsewhere, in the kernel or the system libraries.
sections.plainLanguage: The four cases are walked through in turn. The one the memo recommends is a single program that speaks both, on a machine that has both. It tries IPv6 first if the other end offers it, and falls back to IPv4 automatically. The awkward case is the program that has to run on a machine with no IPv6 at all, where a call that fails because IPv6 is missing has to be ignored rather than treated as fatal.

sections.title: What Has to Change in the Code
sections.content:
The minimum changes needed for IPv4 applications to work with IPv6 come down to the different size and format of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Applications written with IPv4 in mind have many IP dependencies in their source code, and the memo lists the common ones: the presentation format for an IP address, which is an ASCII string, dotted-decimal for IPv4 and hexadecimal for IPv6; the transport layer API, meaning the functions that establish communications and exchange information; name and address resolution, meaning the conversion functions between host names and IP addresses; specific IP dependencies such as address selection, application framing and storage of IP addresses; and multicast applications, which must find the IPv6 equivalents to the IPv4 multicast addresses and use the right socket configuration options.

Presentation format. There are two problems, the memory allocated and the management of the format. The memory allocated to hold an IPv4 address as a string is usually too small for an IPv6 address, and applications should be modified to prevent buffer overflows made possible by the larger address. IPv4 uses a dot to separate four octets in decimal notation, and IPv6 uses a colon to separate each pair of octets in hexadecimal notation. Where a port number has to be given with the address, it may be desirable to put the address inside square brackets. IPv4 often couples the address and port with a colon, for example 192.0.2.1:80, but that would be ambiguous with IPv6, where colons already structure the address, so parsers that take a port number separated by a colon should distinguish IPv6 addresses somehow, for example by enclosing the address in brackets as is done in URLs, for example http://[2001:db8::1]:80. A prefix length should go outside the square brackets, as in [2001:db8::]/64 or 2001:db8::/64 and not [2001:db8::/64]. In some cases a zone identifier may be needed as part of the address, for example fe80::1%eth0, though in general applications should not need to parse those identifiers. Parsers should support the bracketed form even when no port number is used, and requiring the user always to give a bracketed literal is not recommended. Some applications represent IPv6 address literals differently, SMTP for example uses [IPv6:2001:db8::1]. The use of address literals is strongly discouraged for general-purpose direct input; host names and DNS should be used instead.

Transport layer API. When an application is ported to IPv6, most changes belong in its transport module, which manages everything related to communications and uses the transport-layer API, typically a network library. Four things need review. Network information storage: the new structures must hold 128-bit IP addresses, and the use of generic address structures that can store any address family is recommended. Special addresses hard-coded in the source need attention, in particular the wildcard local, loopback and broadcast addresses, and since IPv6 has no broadcast address applications can use multicast instead. Address conversion functions, which convert between the binary address representation and the presentation format, have new versions specified for the IPv6 address format. The communication API functions keep the same signatures, based on a generic socket address structure, and the same functions are valid for IPv6, but the address data structures used when calling them need updating. The network configuration options, used when different communication models are configured for input and output operations such as blocking or non-blocking and I/O multiplexing, should be translated for IPv6.

Name and address resolution. With IPv6 there are two new basic resolution functions, getaddrinfo() and getnameinfo(). The first returns a list of all the configured IP addresses for a host name. The queries can be constrained to one protocol family, for instance only IPv4 or only IPv6, but it is recommended that all configured IP addresses be obtained, so that the application works with every kind of node. The second returns the host name associated with an IP address.

Specific IP dependencies. Unlike the IPv4 model, IPv6 promotes the configuration of multiple IP addresses per node, while applications use only a destination and source pair for a communication, so choosing the right pair may determine the route the datagrams take. Nodes, not applications, normally solve source address selection, following rules of best choice from RFC 3484, while allowing applications to change the ordering rules. For the destination, applications ask the resolver, which returns a set of valid addresses; unless they have a specific reason to pick one, they should try each element in the list until the communication succeeds. If an application has to specify its source address, the destination selection process picks the best destination for that source address instead of the other way round, which adds complexity for version-independent applications, though specifying a source address is not typically required. Application framing is the next dependency: applications using connectionless protocols such as UDP typically need it, and have three choices, to use packet sizes no larger than the IPv6 minimum Maximum Transmission Unit of 1280 bytes, to use any packet sizes but force IPv6 fragmentation and reassembly when necessary, or to optimize the packet size and avoid unnecessary fragmentation by guessing or finding out the optimal sizes that can be sent and received end to end. The memo takes no stance on which approach is best, and notes that the optimal choice depends on dynamic factors such as Path MTU and whether IPv4 or IPv6 is being used. Finally, applications should not store IP addresses. Addresses change over time, for instance after renumbering, and the same node can reach a destination host using different addresses, possibly with a different protocol version. Where possible, applications should store names such as FQDNs or other protocol-independent identities, and be bound to specific addresses only at run time or for the duration of a cache lifetime. Peer-to-peer systems may need to cache addresses for performance, but cached addresses should not be treated as permanent, reliable information.

Multicast applications. Two changes are needed: the IPv4 multicast addresses become IPv6 ones, and the socket configuration options change. All IPv6 multicast addresses encode scope, where in IPv4 the scope was only implicit, with multicast groups in 239/8. Although a large number of application-specific multicast addresses were assigned with IPv4, this was avoided with IPv6, so there are no direct equivalents for all of the IPv4 multicast addresses. For link-local multicast it is possible to pick almost anything within the link-local scope, and global groups could use unicast prefix-based addresses as described in RFC 3306. This may force developers to write more protocol-dependent code. IPv6 multicast also does not yet have a standardized mechanism for traditional Any Source Multicast for interdomain multicast, and it may be beneficial to port applications to use SSM semantics, which requires off-band source discovery mechanisms and a different API. A generic problem with multiparty conferencing applications is that all users of the session must use the same protocol version, or some form of proxy or translator.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the work is in four places: the code that turns an address into text, the socket calls, the name lookup, and the places that store an address for later. The address text changes shape and gets longer, so buffers have to grow. The lookup changes to functions that return a list of addresses instead of one. And anything that remembers an address for later has to remember a name instead, because addresses change.

sections.title: Writing Version-Independent Applications
sections.content:
Dual applications, working with both IPv4 and IPv6, are recommended. They should avoid IP dependencies in the source code, and if IP dependencies are required, one of the better solutions is to build a communication library that provides an IP version-independent API to applications and hides all the dependencies.

All memory structures and APIs should be IP version-independent. The memo says to avoid struct in_addr, struct in6_addr, struct sockaddr_in and struct sockaddr_in6. If a network address is passed to a function and one uses struct in_addr or struct in6_addr, the result is an extra parameter to indicate the address family, and a call for the IPv4 case looks like foo(&in4addr, AF_INET) against foo(&in6addr, AF_INET6) for the IPv6 case. That leads to duplicated code and to having to consider each scenario from both perspectives independently, which is difficult to maintain. The answer is struct sockaddr_storage, which works for either family.

On the API side, the new address-independent variants getaddrinfo() and getnameinfo() hide the details of name-to-address and address-to-name translations. They implement the functionality of gethostbyname(), gethostbyaddr(), getservbyname() and getservbyport(), and they obsolete the functionality of gethostbyname2(). They can perform host name and address, and service name and port, lookups at once. getaddrinfo() can return multiple addresses, as the memo shows for a host with three addresses: an IPv4 pair and an IPv6 one. If IPv6 is preferred, getaddrinfo returns the IPv6 address first, and then the two IPv4 addresses in a random order. Hardcoding address-family-dependent knowledge in the program is not preferred: constructs that switch on the address family to work out a length should be avoided in favour of the ai_addrlen member of the addrinfo structure, as returned by getaddrinfo().

The memo then shows two examples of overly simplistic code, one for a TCP server and one for a TCP client, each of which uses the first result from getaddrinfo() and stops there. The comments in the code list what can go wrong: a server that ends up IPv4 only, IPv6 only, or absent altogether, and a client that tries the first address and, if it fails, falls back to a timeout rather than to the next record.

The correct approach is an iterated job. In client code, when multiple addresses are returned from getaddrinfo(), all of them should be tried until the connection succeeds, and when a failure occurs with socket(), connect(), bind() or some other function, the code should go on to the next address. If something is wrong with the socket call because the address family is not supported, the application should try the next address structure. The server example loops over the results, creates a socket for each, sets IPV6_V6ONLY on the IPv6 socket where the address family is AF_INET6, and skips the EAFNOSUPPORT and EPROTONOSUPPORT errors until the last address family. The client example loops over the results, continues on a failed connect, and breaks out of the loop as soon as one connect succeeds.

The memo's security considerations say that the security issues of IPv6 transition are outside its scope, but that cycling through addresses until a working one is found is what keeps the service available during the transition. It also flags IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses as a mixed blessing: they make application transition easier, but they are hard to police, and some systems disable them by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the socket calls that take any kind of address, and use the lookup that returns a list of addresses rather than one. Then loop over that list: try each address in turn, move on when one fails, and stop at the first that works. On a server, do the same over the addresses to listen on.

layers.label: Application
layers.detail: appv4, appv6, or appv4/v6: the program that sends and receives the data

layers.label: Transport protocols
layers.detail: TCP, UDP, SCTP, DCCP and others

layers.label: IP
layers.detail: IPv4, IPv6, or both, depending on what the node has enabled

viz.caption: THE FOUR CASES OF APPLICATION TRANSITION

items.title: Case 1
items.text: IPv4-only applications in a dual-stack node. The node has both protocol stacks, but the applications have not been ported.

items.title: Case 2
items.text: IPv4-only and IPv6-only applications in a dual-stack node. Two similar applications, one for each protocol version, for example ping and ping6.

items.title: Case 3
items.text: Applications supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 in a dual-stack node. The IPv4-only applications can be removed. The memo calls this the most advisable case.

items.title: Case 4
items.text: Applications supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 in an IPv4-only node, where the same program has to work with IPv6 disabled or absent.
